extracted.intended_audience: patent applicants, patent attorneys, and patent office officials handling deposits of biological material
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and quality/procedural requirements for depositing biological material for patent applications (what must be deposited, when, where, how to document it, storage and access conditions, and replacement/transfer rules) across national patent offices. Covers obligations under the Budapest Treaty and corresponding national implementations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposits must comply with the Budapest Treaty
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposits shall be in accordance with the provisions of the Budapest Treaty on the International Recognition of the Deposit of Biological Material for the Purposes of Patent Procedure; WIPO publishes a list of internationally recognized depositaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many national provisions refer explicitly to the Budapest Treaty and require deposit at institutions recognized under it; where national law has no specific storage/availability rules, Budapest Treaty standards apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to deposit when invention involves non-public biological material
rubrics_metrics.description: Where an invention involves biological material that is not available to the public or cannot be described sufficiently in the application to enable a skilled person to carry out the invention, a sample/culture must be deposited (or reference to an earlier deposit may form part of the description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Italy, Lithuania, Mexico, Japan and other jurisdictions specify that deposit is obligatory in such cases; definition varies but generally means material 'not available to the public' and not reproducible from the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must identify deposit details and relevant characteristics
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent specification/application must state the authorized depositary authority, the deposit number and the date of deposit, and relevant information about the characteristics of the biological material that are available to the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy, Mexico, Netherlands, Lithuania and others require these details in the description. Netherlands further requires a depositor's written statement describing properties, handling, cultivation and identification references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of deposit — general rule: by filing date (or priority date)
rubrics_metrics.description: The deposit must be made not later than the filing date of the patent application or, where priority is claimed, not later than the priority date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is stated explicitly for many jurisdictions (Iceland Art.8(6); Italy; Netherlands; Lithuania; India) as the default requirement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted late filing of deposit information within country-specific time-limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Several jurisdictions permit the deposit record or deposit information to be submitted within a specified period after filing (e.g., Mexico: within six months; Latvia: with application or no later than three months; Netherlands: number/receipt may be furnished within one month; Italy: information may be provided within 16 months in certain cases).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions and effects differ by country: Mexico ties late submission to preservation of original filing date (if deposit occurred before filing); failure to submit within the period can result in abandonment or change of filing date. Italy allows 16 months in line with Budapest/PCT timing in some cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notification to patent office of deposit and deposit number (timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant has deposited biological material, they shall inform the national patent office in writing of the institution and deposit number within a prescribed time (e.g., Iceland: within 16 months of filing or priority; Italy: may provide within 16 months or earlier if early publication/availability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If applicant requests early publication or early public availability, the information must be provided at latest when the request is submitted. Transfers between depositaries must also be notified as soon as possible after receipt of transfer receipt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Documentation/receipt requirements for filing
rubrics_metrics.description: A copy of the receipt issued by the depositary (showing deposit details) or a document confirming the deposit must be attached to or submitted with the application (or within the permitted time limit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Japan requires attachment of a copy of the latest receipt (Rule 27bis) unless microorganism readily available. Netherlands and Lithuania require copy of receipt or deposit confirmation; Nethelands permits submission within one month.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accepted depositaries — recognized international or designated national institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposits must be made with an international depositary authority recognized under the Budapest Treaty or with national institutions designated/recognized by the national patent office in accordance with the Treaty/ national rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mexico, Netherlands and other countries state that only international depositary authorities or patent-office-designated institutions are acceptable; national lists or Gazettes may publish recognized institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duration of storage — minimum/term rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Depositaries shall store deposited biological material for prescribed periods (commonly at least 30 years for international deposits; national deposits sometimes stored until expiration of patent; some rules add at least five years after most recent request).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy cites Budapest Treaty/Rule 9.1: minimum five years after last request and in any case 30 years from date of deposit; Netherlands requires at least 30 years; Japan: national deposits until patent expiration, international at least 30 years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of availability of samples (when samples may be furnished)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules specify when a sample becomes available for furnishing — e.g., from the date the application is open to public inspection (normally 18 months) until grant; or from the date of filing; or from time of registration/establishment of patent right with limited exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Italy: available from public inspection (normally 18 months after filing) until grant (or 20 years from filing if application rejected/withdrawn). Netherlands: available from filing date for furnishing until it is certain no patent will be granted or until patent has lost effect. Japan: generally from registration, with limited earlier access in specific circumstances (written warning for commercial working; applicant who received notice of refusal).

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on furnishing — permitted uses and prohibition on transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: Furnishing of samples is restricted to experimental/research purposes; released samples may not be transferred to third parties and must be used only for the declared research purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Japan and many national rules state samples are for experiments/research and may not be transferred. Italy and others require undertakings that culture be used only through a named qualified expert and not made available to third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Restrictions on recipients — independent/qualified experts and applicant-imposed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants may request that samples be provided only to independent experts or qualified named experts; national offices lay down requirements for who qualifies as an independent expert and may require approval of the expert by applicant/patent holder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland: applicant may demand samples be supplied only to independent experts until grant, and in some circumstances for 20 years after filing if application refused/withdrawn; Italy requires named qualified expert and holds expert responsible for abuses; Regulation Art.48 requires requests and expert undertakings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undertakings and written declarations required from requesters/experts
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for samples must be filed in writing and accompanied by a declaration/undertaking to observe restrictions (use only for research, not allow others access, apply same undertakings to derived cultures). If expert is to receive the sample, the expert must give the declaration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland Art.22(6)-(8) and Art.47/48 detail that requesters must undertake to use samples only for research until final decision, not allow others access, and sign declarations. Italy similarly requires undertakings; Netherlands requires irrevocable permission statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant/patent holder may limit availability following refusal/withdrawal
rubrics_metrics.description: If an application has been refused/dismissed or considered withdrawn, the applicant may, for a specified period (e.g., 20 years from filing), demand that samples be supplied only to independent experts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland and Italy explicitly provide a 20-year protection period after filing in such circumstances; national Ministers or offices may issue rules on time-limits and who counts as independent experts.

rubrics_metrics.name: New deposit/replacement when original sample becomes inactive or unavailable
rubrics_metrics.description: If deposited biological material becomes inactive or cannot be supplied, it may be exchanged with a sample of the same culture within prescribed time and procedures; in some cases the new deposit is considered to have been made on the same date as the previous deposit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland allows exchange with same-date effect per Art.8(7). Regulation Art.46: new deposit must comply with Budapest Treaty and be made within three months of depositor receiving notice of non-availability; special nine-month rule if depositary ceased operations and depositor had no knowledge. Netherlands allows new deposit within three months after notification and requires depositor statement that new deposit is identical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deposit of derived samples for new applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Deposit of a sample derived from a specimen previously provided is permitted for a new patent application if deposit of the derived sample is necessary for the new application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation Art.49 explicitly permits derived-sample deposits despite prior statements restricting provision, provided necessary for the new application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safety and authorization limitations on furnishing
rubrics_metrics.description: Samples shall not be supplied to persons who are unauthorized by regulation or who, due to the harmful properties of the material, are considered incompetent to process the sample without considerable risk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland Art.22(6) states that regulatory or safety prohibitions bar furnishing; offices may refuse supply on safety grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural formality reference to Budapest Treaty Rules (e.g., Rule 11) and appeal rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests for provision of samples shall be presented in accordance with the relevant Rules under the Budapest Treaty (for example Rule 11), and national offices may issue statements or refuse and such decisions can be appealed to national Boards/Appeals within specified time-limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Iceland Art.47/50 references Rule 11 and allows referral to Board of Appeal within two months. Many national provisions direct that presentation/processing follow Treaty regulations and national procedural statutes.
